US.71.def: Office and professional occupations (managers, salespeople, clerks) that grew rapidly in the 1950s, outnumbering factory workers for the first time.
The 1950s American dream of owning a single-family home in the suburbs with a yard, garage, and modern appliances, drawing families out of cities.
The Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944, which gave veterans college tuition, home loans, and job training, creating a massive new middle class.
The 1950s economic culture of buying goods beyond basic needs—televisions, cars, appliances, homes—driving growth and defining postwar life.
The first mass-produced suburb, built by William Levitt on Long Island starting in 1947 using assembly-line techniques to build homes quickly and cheaply.
America’s growing reliance on imported petroleum from the Middle East to fuel its car-centered economy, creating vulnerabilities in the 1970s.

US.72.def: The dramatic increase in birth rates from 1946–1964, when 76 million babies were born, transforming the American economy and culture as they grew up.
An economy driven by high household spending on homes, cars, and appliances — powered in the 1950s by postwar prosperity and Baby Boom families.
The mass 1950s movement of families to newly built suburbs, driven by cheap housing, automobiles, and growing Baby Boom households.
The large new consumer market of children and teenagers created by the Baby Boom, targeted by toy, music, food, and clothing industries.
The 1950s ideal household of a married couple and their children, celebrated in advertising and television as the American norm.
The broad economic growth and rising standard of living the United States enjoyed after World War II.

US.73.def: Massive 41,000-mile highway network authorized by President Eisenhower in 1956 that transformed American travel, commerce, and settlement patterns.
The vaccine developed by Dr. Jonas Salk, announced safe in April 1955, that ended the epidemic that had paralyzed or killed thousands of children yearly.
The 34th U.S. President (1953–1961) and former WWII general who ended the Korean War and launched the Interstate Highway System.
The close relationship between the armed forces and defense industries that Eisenhower warned about in his 1961 farewell address.
Eisenhower's policy of avoiding direct war with the Soviet Union while containing communism through deterrence and diplomacy.
The weakening of inner cities as highways and suburbs pulled residents and businesses away — an unintended consequence of the Interstate system.

US.74.def: The 1950s American dream of owning a single-family home in the suburbs with a yard, garage, and modern appliances, drawing families out of cities.
Massive 41,000-mile highway network authorized by President Eisenhower in 1956 that transformed American travel, commerce, and settlement patterns.
The 1950s lifestyle centered on cars, which symbolized freedom and prosperity, reshaping cities, suburbs, and daily life across America.
Restaurant businesses like McDonald’s that used assembly-line prep and drive-through service to feed automobile travelers quickly and cheaply.
Standardized roadside lodging like Holiday Inn, founded 1952, built along highways to serve automobile travelers with predictable quality and amenities.
The first mass-produced suburb, built by William Levitt on Long Island starting in 1947 using assembly-line techniques to build homes quickly and cheaply.

US.75.def: The electronic medium that became the dominant form of American entertainment and information by the late 1950s, creating shared national experiences.
Communication channels—TV, radio, newspapers, magazines—that reach large audiences at once; in the 1950s television became the most powerful medium.
The rapidly growing 1950s industry that used television to shape consumer desires and sell products to mass audiences.
A society centered on buying goods; 1950s television and advertising encouraged Americans to define success through purchases.
The way national television gave Americans shared programs, products, and values, making regional cultures more alike.
The first televised presidential debates (1960), which showed television's new power to shape politics and public opinion.

US.76.def: Members of the 1950s Beat Generation—writers like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg—who rejected mainstream culture, materialism, and conformity.
Revolutionary 1950s music genre combining rhythm and blues, country, and gospel; Elvis Presley became its “King,” representing youth rebellion.
Tennessee singer who became “The King of Rock ’n’ Roll” in the 1950s, revolutionizing popular culture and launching rock as a global phenomenon.
Memphis recording studio where Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis, and others recorded, creating the “Memphis Sound” of rock ’n’ roll.
Memphis record label founded 1957, legendary for soul music and home to Otis Redding and Isaac Hayes, putting Tennessee at the center of American music.
Mississippi-born blues guitarist who recorded in Memphis and became “King of the Blues,” shaping rock, soul, and popular music from Tennessee.

US.77.def: President John F. Kennedy’s 1960s domestic program promoting economic growth, education, civil rights, and space exploration; a symbol of optimism.
Volunteer program created by President Kennedy in 1961, sending Americans to developing countries to help with education, health, and economic development.
President Kennedy’s 1961 pledge to land Americans on the moon before 1970, mobilizing national resources, advancing technology, and inspiring a generation.
The Cold War competition between the U.S. and Soviet Union to achieve firsts in space exploration; a top New Frontier priority.
The 35th U.S. President (1961–1963) whose New Frontier promised progress in civil rights, the economy, and space.
The NASA program launched under Kennedy's goal of landing an American on the Moon before the decade's end.
